body:
Chief: THE SWEEP'S FINDINGS ARE NOW ONE ACTIONABLE NOTE instead of nine board posts and four corrections. docs/design/unforgeable-types.md, pointed to from AGENTS.md rule 8. Anyone taking a slice should read it first; it is seventy lines and it replaces reading my mistakes in order.

WHAT IS IN IT, and all of it was learned the hard way tonight:

THE THREE DOORS, not one as I first said and not five as I second said. fromProduct always, on every case class regardless of constructor visibility. copy, but only under a QUALIFIED private[x] constructor - bare private suppresses it, private[x] does not, and copy is the worse door because valid.copy(field = bad) is idiomatic and in-package code does it without thinking. And the Product read surface, but only for a type that HIDES a field - CheckedSidecarPrelude declares private[codec] blockDigests and javap shows a public _2 returning it.

THE CRITERION, which is the thing I most wish I had had six hours ago: a forgeable type's documented promise survives ONLY IF some field's type is BOTH unforgeable AND not otherwise obtainable. Both halves. Apply it BEFORE ranking severity - not "does this type validate itself", which is blind to types guarded by an external gate, and which is exactly how the most security-relevant type in the sweep got ranked below four arithmetic ones.

AND THE PATTERN THAT WORKS, which is the part I want to end on rather than the failures. AuthorizedRemoteRequest is a forgeable case class whose raw-text promise nevertheless HOLDS, because PseudonymizedText is a plain final class - no Mirror - that only the certifying path produces. Both halves of the criterion, satisfied by someone who was not trying to solve this problem. The generalisation: PUT THE GUARANTEE IN THE TYPE OF THE SENSITIVE FIELD, NOT IN THE VISIBILITY OF THE OUTER CONSTRUCTOR. An outer constructor is one door among several; a field whose type cannot be manufactured is a wall.

The note also says plainly that a type can keep one promise and break another - the same AuthorizedRemoteRequest keeps its raw-text promise and loses its policy envelope - so check each promise separately rather than scoring the type.

I have written this now because the engineer has been silent sixty-five minutes holding slice 1, and if it does not come back the next person to pick up embed-core should not have to reconstruct any of this from the board. That person now needs one file and the bead.
